14:52 · clip in, demo page out

Break down the reference clip

Prompts you sent
m2-res_174p.mp4how to do an animation like this in CSS and HTML/JS?
I wanna see a html that running and show these animations
Assets in
  • m2-res_174p.mp432 s · 230×174 · 30 fps

What happened

  1. Pulled frames with ffmpeg at 1 and 2 frames per second and tiled them into contact sheets to read the sequence.
  2. Split it into nine beats: screen dive, runway tunnel, glyph tunnel, light burst, charging orb, shell burst, bokeh and smoke, name card, dive and rise.
  3. Chose one technique per beat (table below), using CSS where gradients and transforms do the job and canvas where there are hundreds of moving pieces.
  4. Built one HTML file with no libraries. A single render(t) function places every layer, so the timeline can be scrubbed, slowed down or captured frame by frame.
  5. Used original stand-ins for the device and the glyph alphabet, with TAMAGO / タマゴ as placeholder text.
  6. Rendered 20 timestamps in headless Chromium, compared them with the clip, then fixed the runway shape, the disk texture and the text density.
BeatTechnique
Screen diveCSS 3D: perspective, rotateX easing to 0, a scale() ramp
Runway tunnelrepeating-radial-gradient rings offset by a CSS variable; a striped plane at rotateX(72deg)
Glyph tunnelCanvas 2D: 26 rings × 16 glyph sprites, projected with x·f/z
Light burstThree repeating-conic-gradient spoke layers, a radial mask, mix-blend-mode: screen
Charging orbStacked gradients; color-mix() shifts it from blue to gold
Shell burst900 canvas particles at p₀ + v·age + ½g·age²
Bokeh & smokeSoft sprites drawn with globalCompositeOperation = "lighter"
Name cardSpinning conic texture, SVG feTurbulence displacement, scaleY(.54); text rows at different speeds
Dive & risetranslateY and scale tween; canvas warp streaks
 
// the whole page runs off one number
function frame(now) {
  const dt = Math.min(.05, (now - last) / 1000); last = now;
  if (playing && !scrubbing) { T += dt * speed; if (T >= D) T -= D; }
  render(T);                     // every layer is a pure function of T
  requestAnimationFrame(frame);
}
Output

Tamago Hatch Sequence: a 32-second loop with play, pause, 0.25× to 1× speed, a scrubber and a chip for each scene.

Reusable version
Here's a 32-second reference clip. Break it into beats and rebuild it as one self-contained HTML page with CSS and canvas, no libraries. Drive every layer from a single time value so I can scrub it, and caption each scene with the technique it uses.

18:49 · photo in, cutout and new name out

Swap in the real Digivice

Prompt you sent
I have this digivice image, can you trim this and use it as png? then update the "Tamago" to "Tonkatsudon".

What happened

  1. Removed the white background: flood-filled the near-white pixels connected to the border, shrank the mask by 1 px, feathered it, and removed the white fringe from the edge pixels.
  2. Cropped to 1127×994 with a transparent background, then checked the edges on dark and green.
  3. Measured the screen centre in the cutout (49.87% across, 49.3% down) and made it the transform-origin, so every rotate and scale lands on the LCD.
  4. Stacked four darker copies behind the PNG with translateZ, which shows as thickness when it tilts.
  5. Added a glowing LCD layer that powers up between 0.9 s and 1.9 s, just before the dive.
  6. Changed the name card to TONKATSUDON / トンカツドン.
.dev{ width:62vmin; aspect-ratio:1127/994;
  transform-origin:49.87% 49.3%;   /* the LCD centre, so the zoom lands in the screen */
  transform-style:preserve-3d }
.dev .e1{ transform:translateZ(-.5vmin) }   /* …down to .e4 at -2vmin: darker copies = thickness */
Output

digivice.png (1127×994, transparent) and the Tamago page with the real device and the new name.

Reusable version
Cut this product photo out of its white background as a transparent PNG. Put it in scene 1 so the camera flies into its screen, using the screen centre as the transform origin. Change the name text to Tonkatsudon / トンカツドン, and embed the image so the page stays a single file.

18:53 · bug report in, self-contained page out

Fix the missing image

Prompt you sent
screenshot.pngit doesn't show the actual image
Assets in
  • screenshot.png734×642 · empty image boxes

What happened

  1. The page loaded the PNG by a relative path, digivice.png. Where it was opened, that file wasn't found, so the browser drew empty boxes with only their outlines and alt text.
  2. Moved the PNG into the page as a base64 data URI, defined once as a CSS variable in a style block at the end of the file.
  3. Turned the five image layers into divs that use that variable as their background, so the data appears only once.
  4. Rendered the dive again with no PNG anywhere nearby to confirm it loads.
.dev .pic{ background:var(--digivice) center/100% 100% no-repeat }

/* one style block at the very end of the file */
:root{ --digivice:url("data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgo…") }
LessonBuild small assets into the page. A single file works the same whether it's published, downloaded, or opened straight from disk.
Output

tamago-hatch.html, 1.2 MB, with no outside files.

Reusable version
The image shows as an empty box. Make the page self-contained so it works both published and opened straight from disk.

19:41 · 3D model in, web-ready model and renderer out

Replace the PNG with a 3D model

Prompt you sent
digivice.glbI have a Digivice.glb for you to use, you can replace the png in the animation
Assets in
  • digivice.glb8.9 MB · 105k tris · 20 PNG textures at 1024 px · CC BY 4.0

What happened

  1. Read the model's structure: six meshes (body, lights, screen, screen corner, buttons, antenna), PBR materials, no compression.
  2. The workspace couldn't reach npm, PyPI, GitHub or the CDNs, so three.js couldn't be loaded for testing. A small WebGL2 renderer with no dependencies was written instead, and it could be tested frame by frame.
  3. Baked the model in Python: removed the node hierarchy, put the screen centre at the origin facing the camera, and scaled the device to 2 units wide.
  4. Shrank it: dropped tangents (the shader rebuilds them), 16-bit indices, 8-bit normals, 16-bit UVs, JPEG textures. 8.9 MB became 1.7 MB gzipped.
  5. Your next message arrived with four more models while this was in progress, so the work carried straight into step 5.
Output

digivice.bin.gz (1.7 MB) and the renderer that steps 4 and 5 share.

Reusable version
Replace the PNG with this GLB. Shrink the model for the web, keep the page self-contained, and fly the camera into its screen.

19:45 · four models in, snap-scroll page out

Two evolutions on a snap-scroll page

Prompt you sent
4 × .glbI have 4 glb files. I want you to do Acumon to Gremon evolution and Gabumon to Garurumon evolution. Make it slower when it evolutions. At the end, I want you to create a snap scroll web page to do the animation when users scroll down the page.
Assets in
  • digimon_agumon.glb1.8 MB
  • mobile_-_digimon_linkz_-_gabumon.glb1.1 MB
  • digimon_greymon.glb38 MB
  • digimon_garurumon.glb35 MB

The step ran as six parts: checking the models, shrinking them, drawing them, timing the evolution, wiring the scroll, then testing.

5aCheck which way each model faces

Before writing any camera moves, each model was drawn as a point cloud from the front, back, side and top. All four face +Z with Y up, so one camera setup works for every character. Gabumon's mesh is stored in a T-pose; its animation clips pose it.

5bShrink the models for the web

Greymon and Garurumon arrived as 73 MB of sculpts with over a million triangles each. Each model was baked in Python into a compact binary, then built into the page as base64 text.

ModelTrianglesCompressedWhat changed
Digivice105k1.70 MBScreen centred at the origin; light-blue tint to match the photo
Agumon26k0.24 MBFlat body colour; only the eye texture kept
Gabumon5k0.33 MBIdle, win and special clips pre-sampled as joint matrices at 24–30 fps
Greymon1.15M → 124k1.15 MBDecimated by vertex clustering; 2.3 units tall
Garurumon1.02M → 134k1.25 MBDecimated by vertex clustering; 1.55 units tall
 
# vertex clustering: one new vertex per occupied grid cell
key = np.floor(P / cell).astype(np.int64)
ids, inv = np.unique(key_1d, return_inverse=True)
NP = cell_means(P, inv)                 # average position (and colour) per cell
NF = inv[F]                             # remap every triangle to the merged vertices
NF = NF[(NF[:,0]!=NF[:,1]) & (NF[:,1]!=NF[:,2]) & (NF[:,0]!=NF[:,2])]   # drop collapsed ones

5cDraw the models and the effects

The renderer is about 300 lines of WebGL2. It draws three kinds of model (textured, vertex-coloured, and Gabumon's skinned mesh) with soft, slightly toon-like lighting. Two extra controls do the evolution: a glow that turns the body into a white-hot silhouette with rising scan lines, and a dissolve that eats through the model by height with a glowing edge.

// dissolve: a noisy height threshold sweeps through the model
float hh = vObj.y / uHeight + (noise(vObj * 22.) - .5) * .28;
float d  = (hh - uDiss) * uDissDir;       // +1 vanishes upward, -1 forms upward
if (d < 0.) discard;
col += uDissCol * (1. - smoothstep(0., .07, d)) * 5.;   // hot edge

Glyph rings, sparks, the light pillar, the glowing LCD and the pedestal disks are flat quads drawn with additive blending, all cut from one texture sheet painted on a canvas at load. Around the 3D canvas sit the 2D and CSS layers from step 1, back to front:

  1. BackdropCSS radial gradient in the scene's colours
  2. Back canvasGlyph tunnel, bokeh, smoke column
  3. RaysCSS conic-gradient spokes
  4. Back name rowsText the character stands in front of
  5. WebGL2Models, glyph rings, sparks, pedestals
  6. Front canvasNear bokeh, screen-blended
  7. Front rows, call-outアグモン進化, the champion's name
  8. Vignette, flash, fadeScene transitions and the reveal flash
  9. Snap scrollerSection headings, replay, nav dots

5dTime the evolution, then slow it down

Both evolutions share one 24-second script. The slow motion comes from a second clock: between 8.2 s and 16.1 s it runs at 0.26× speed, and everything that moves (the spin, rings, particles and Gabumon's idle animation) reads that clock. The fades and cuts stay on real time, so the story keeps its pace while the motion slows.

PhaseTimeWhat happens
Dive0 – 2.45 sThe camera flies into the Digivice screen as the LCD powers up.
Tunnel2.0 – 5.0 sThe glyph tunnel speeds up; white flash at 4.85 s.
Rookie4.8 – 8.1 sAgumon or Gabumon on the pedestal; call-out at 7.0 s.
Evolution8.1 – 16.1 sClock at 0.26×. Silhouette glow, glyph rings, three slow turns. The rookie dissolves 10.2–12.6 s, the champion forms 11.2–14.2 s, flash at 15.9 s.
Reveal16.1 s →The champion on its pedestal with name rows and smoke; it idles until you scroll on.
 
// 1× → 0.26× → 1×, integrated once into a lookup table
const rate = t => 1 - .74 * E.inOut(env(t, 8.2, 16.1, 1.3, .9));
const CLK = new Float32Array(9001);
for (let i = 0; i < 9000; i++) CLK[i + 1] = CLK[i] + rate(i * .01) * .01;
// motion reads clock(t); fades and cuts read t

5eWire the snap scroll

The visuals sit on one fixed stage. On top of it, a full-screen scroller holds four sections: Digivice, Agumon → Greymon, Gabumon → Garurumon, and Partners. When a section is at least 60% in view, its scene fades in and starts from 0 s.

#snap{ position:fixed; inset:0; overflow-y:auto; scroll-snap-type:y mandatory }
section{ height:100%; scroll-snap-align:start; scroll-snap-stop:always }

new IntersectionObserver(entries => {
  for (const e of entries)
    if (e.isIntersecting && e.intersectionRatio >= .6) activate(e.target.dataset.scene);
}, { root: snap, threshold: [.6] });

5fTest, fix, test again

Frames were captured at set times with a small debug hook, digi.seek(scene, t), at desktop (960×600) and phone (390×844) sizes. Scripted runs then tested the wheel, the Home key and the nav dots.

FoundFix
Models didn't load: their data sat below the app scriptStart loading on DOMContentLoaded
White frames in the tunnelA WebGL canvas keeps its last frame, so clear it every frame
Greymon read yellow, the Digivice whiteLower the lights; tint the Digivice to its real light blue
The LCD washed outMake the screen dark glass so the glowing bars read
Name rows too dense, crossing headingsFewer rows, wider gaps, moved below the headings
Scene one step behind the scroll on slow devicesTime the fade by the wall clock, not by frames

20:21 · queued, not built yet

Next: scroll forward, scroll back to rewind

Prompt you sent
I want you to split the animation into small chunk. When I scroll down it animates forward, when I scroll up, it rewinds the animate

This request was interrupted before any work started. The current page is already set up for it: every frame is render(scene, t), so scroll can drive t directly instead of a clock.

  1. Make each evolution section five screens tall and keep the stage pinned while it scrolls past.
  2. Use the five phases (dive, tunnel, rookie, evolution, reveal) as the chunks, with a snap point at the start of each.
  3. Turn scroll progress through the section into t. Scrolling up lowers progress, which rewinds.
  4. Give the evolution chunk more scroll distance than the others, so the slow motion survives.
// inside a tall section with a sticky stage
const p = clamp(-sec.getBoundingClientRect().top / (sec.offsetHeight - innerHeight));
render(scene, p * SCENE_LENGTH);        // scroll down: t grows · scroll up: t shrinks

.chunk{ height:100vh; scroll-snap-align:start }   /* one per phase */
Reusable version
Split each evolution into its five phases and drive them with scroll instead of a timer: scrolling down plays forward, scrolling up rewinds. Snap to the start of each phase, and give the evolution phase the most scroll distance so the slow motion is kept.
